text: And now I give the floor to his
excellency Abdulatif bin Rashid al-
Zayani,
Minister of foreign for foreign affairs
of Bahrain.
In the name of God, the most gracious,
the most merciful. Your Excellency Dr.
Khaled Rahman, President of the United
Nations General Assembly. Your
Excellency Mr. Antonia Gutes, Secretary
General of the United Nations. Ladies
and gentlemen,
peace and blessings of God be upon you.
Allow me to congratulate you,
excellency, on your election as
president of the 81st session of the
general assembly. I wish you every
success in conducting the work of this
session. We would like to express the
Kingdom of Bahrain's appreciation to
your brotherly country, the People's
Republic of Bangladesh, as well as the
Secretary General, for his tireless
efforts in the service of international
peace and security and the sustainable
development goals.
It is my honor to convey to this
distinguished gathering the greetings of
his majesty Kinghammed bin Isa al-
Khalifa, King of the Kingdom of Bahrain
and of his Royal Highness Prince Salman
bin al- Khalifa, Crown Prince and Prime
Minister
and their best wishes for the success of
the session.
Mr. President,
you have chosen for this session a theme
that speaks directly to the challenges
before us. Restoring trust,
managing transformation,
and a united Nations that delivers for
all.
Trust is not restored through statements
or by repeating appeals. Instead, it is
restored by upholding the law and
translating the decisions of this
organization into effective protection
for people's lives, rights, and
livelihoods.
We meet at a time when the Arab Gulf is
facing a security situation of a
severity not witnessed in decades. The
states of the Gulf Corporation Council
and the Hashimite Kingdom of Jordan have
been subjected to waves of unjustified
Iranian attacks involving ballistic
missiles and drones
targeting civilian infrastructure,
residential areas, ports, airports and
energy facilities.
This came in flagrant violation of
international law and the charter of the
United Nations.
These are indiscriminate attacks without
justification under any law. My country
also condemns the attacks carried out by
the Iranbacked terrorist Houthi militia
against civilian objects and Islamic
holy sites in the brotherly kingdom of
Saudi Arabia. We also condemn their
threats to freedom of navigation in the
Babel Mandubab and the Red Sea.
Allow me to put the facts before you in
figures. Our countries have been
subjected to nearly 7,000
attack
at the hands of Iran involving 1,700
ballistic missiles, 80 cruise missiles,
drones,
2,000 cargo vessels and tankers with
seaf farers on board have also been
detained while 72 commercial vessels
have been targeted resulting in the
deaths of 22 seaf farers. These are not
merely numbers. Behind every figure is a
ship, a port, a market, and families
waiting for those that provide for them
to return home.
Commercial vessels have been targeted in
the Straits of Hormuz.
Mines have been laid in an international
shipping lane.
Restrictions
on passage have been imposed
in contravention of international law.
The consequences
of all the above extend far beyond the
Arabian Gulf.
It affects energy and food prices,
shipping and insurance costs as well as
supply chains across the world.
As the kingdom renews its full
solidarity with the brotherly countries
subjected to these attacks,
it commends the professionalism
of the Bahrain defense force and the air
defense forces of brotherly countries
and their readiness in confronting these
attacks. We reaffirm the right of all
states to take all lawful measures to
defend their sovereignty and territorial
integrity
pursuant to article 51 of the UN charter
and the joint defense agreement of the
GCC states.
All the same, we continue to exercise
the utmost restraint
seeking to ensure that security and
peace prevail for the benefit of the
people of the region. Mr. President,
the position of the Kingdom of Bahrain
is grounded in international law,
the rights of people's
and
the Strait of Harris is an international
straight and the right of transit
through it is established for the
vessels of all states under the UN
convention on the law of the sea.
That right may not be suspended or
obstructed, nor may it be subjected to
conditions imposed unilaterally by any
state. Accordingly, the kingdom
categorically rejects any permit or fee
regime imposed on the passage.
It rejects the use of international
waterways as instruments of pressure or
economic co urgent or any attempt at the
seizure of vessels. Such actions would
set an extremely dangerous precedent
because what is accepted today in one
strait
may be demanded tomorrow in every
international waterway
upon which global trade depends.
Alternative routes cannot be treated as
a solution to conduct that that violates
international law. Mitigation measures
are an emergency response. They should
not be used as a pretext to claim that
the state is no longer necessary or to
accept a new status quo. The right of
passage does not cease to exist because
alternatives are available. nor does a
violation cease
uh just because the those affected have
found ways to reduce the loss. This
threat is not confined to the straits of
harms. Security Council resolution 2817
also referred to Babel Mendab
recognizing that a threat to one
waterway is a threat to navigation
through all waterways.
The security of navigation in the Red
Sea, the Gulf of Aiden and the Babel
Mandub
is part of the same system. We are now
defending
a regional interest, but a rule that
applies to every international waterway.
And if it does apply to one to our
strait alone, it wouldn't have been a
rule.
The Kingdom of Bahin has not only stated
its position in principle on behalf of
the Gulf Cooperation Council states and
the Hashimite Kingdom of Jordan and by
virtue of its current presidency of the
GCC and its non-permanent membership of
the security council. Bahrain led
efforts resulting in the adoption of
Security Council resolution 2817
with a historic and unprecedented
support of 136 countries. The resolution
condemned the attacks against our
countries, reaffirming their sovereignty
and rejecting any action intended to
close the straight or obstruct
navigation through it.
The kingdom also introduced a draft
resolution under chapter 7 of the
charter to protect commercial
navigation.
The resolution adopted by the council of
the international maritime organization
on the 19th of March together with the
human rights council resolution 61
both have further demonstrated that the
international
rejection of such conduct extends beyond
the security council.
We stress the need for the full
implementation of these resolutions
to ensure that those responsible are
held accountable and there are
compensation for the damage caused. On
the 17th of this month, the kingdom
convened an a formula meeting of the
security council dedicated to freedom of
navigation.
In this session, we heard from 53
affected states,
the maritime transport sector and
relevant international bodies.
And we
heard a conclusion expressed by all
delegations that is freedom of passage
through international straits is a
prerequisite for global economic
prosperity.
The kingdom contributes
to the protection of a rules-based
maritime order across an area exceeding
3 million square miles
through its hosting
in Manama of the headquarters of the
combined maritime forces.
This comprises 47 nations.
We welcome the establishment of the
multinational maritime defense alliance
led by the brotherly kingdom of Saudi
Arabia. The kingdom is proud to
participate
in the alliance as a founding member and
supportive efforts to safeguard
international trade routes and global
energy supplies in accordance with
international law.
As efforts continue in the security
council, this general assembly has an
equally important role to play as the
forum in which all states stand equal.
From this podium, we call upon member
states to support a
firm collective position which upholds
freedom of navigation and the right of
transit passage in accordance with
international law.
It should also affirm that the security
of maritime passages is a collective
responsibility that cannot be subjected
to bilateral arrangements.
This is what restoring trust means in
practice.
This is not a call dictated by the
present crisis. His Royal Highness,
Prince Salman bin Muhammad al- Khalifa,
Crown Prince and Prime Minister,
said from this very podium two years ago
that the systems established to
safeguard the international order were
under severe strain.
He noted that this organization must
evolve to confront the growing threats.
He called for comprehensive
consensusbased
reform encompassing all decision-making
bodies including the security council.
What has happened since then has not
altered that conviction. Instead, it has
reinforced it. Mr. President,
the test of the United Nations
credibility is not only confined to our
waters. The Palestinian calls remains at
the heart of our concerns. The kingdom
reaffirms its steadfast position in
support of the establishment of an
independent
and geographically contiguous state of
Palestine, living side by side with the
state of Israel in peace and security.
The kingdom has also joined the border
of peace as a founding member pursuant
to security council resolution 2803.
This reaffirms our unwavering support
for the rights of the brotherly
Palestinian people.
The kingdom also reaffirms its support
for the unity, sovereignty, and
territorial integrity of the Syrian Arab
Republic, as well as for efforts to lift
sanctions in a manner that enables the
brotherly Syrian people to rebuild their
country. In Sudan, we call for an
immediate ceasefire, the protection of
civilians, unhindered humanitarian
access, and a political solution that
preserves Sudan's unity and in the state
institutions. Turning to Yemen, we renew
our support for a political solution
under United Nations opices led by the
legitimate government. We appreciate the
efforts of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
in this vein.
Our position on other conflicts
including the conflict in Ukraine
is guided by the same principles
regardless of the parties involved. That
is adherence to the charter, respect for
sovereignty and territorial integrity
and the peaceful settlement of disputes.
Mr. for president. The kingdom of
Bahrain,
where mosques, churches, and temples
have stood side by side for generations,
believes that tolerance and coexistence
are not simply policies to be adopted.
Instead, they are the identity of the
Bahraini society and the foundation of
our national unity.
Thus,
we have introduced the initiative
adopted by the general assembly
designating the 28th of January as the
international day of peaceful
coexistence. His majesty the king also
issued the kingdom of Bahrain's
declaration on religious freedom and
freedom of belief.
The King Hammed Global Center for
Coexistence and tolerance was later
established and the King Hammed Award
for Coexistence and tolerance was
launched.
The same approach underpins our
development journey.
The kingdom continues to advance its
economic vision 2030,
pursue its commitment to achieving the
sustainable development goals and
strengthen the status and advancement of
Bahraini women.
The kingdom embraces the women peace and
security agenda
and the youth peace and security agenda.
both our priorities during our
membership in the security council.
No discussion of development today is
complete without addressing the
technology that is reshaping that
development. From this podium two years
ago, his royal highness, the crown
prince and prime minister called for the
adoption of an international treaty
governing the development of artificial
intelligence. It would ensure that this
technology contributes to peace rather
than exacerbating conflict.
Since then, the General Assembly has
taken positive steps.
However, dialogue can bring positions
closer, but it is not
a step that creates obligations. The aim
is not to hold the technology that no
one has the power to hold but to ensure
that its growth is surrounded by
safeguards.
Uh just as the international community
surrounded nuclear energy with
safeguards that preserved its benefits
without preventing it, this technology
knows no borders.
A safeguard adopted by a single state is
not a safeguard just as a rule that
applies in a single state is not a rule.
Therefore, we renew our call for a
binding international
framework to ensure that this technology
becomes a driver of innovation rather
than division. And this in our view is
what it means to manage the
transformation that you chose as a theme
of this session. Mr. President,
all these issues,
however far apart they may seem, are
bound by one fundamental truth. Security
and prosperity are not two parallel
objectives. Instead, they are one single
objective pursued along two paths. There
can be no prosperity without security
and no sustainable security without
interconnected economies and societies
in peace. This is not a Gulf perspective
dictated by our geography.
Instead, it's a lesson that humanity has
learned from its wars. A lesson that
Europe learned when it built its peace
not through treaties alone but on
interests so intertwined that separating
them became costlier than preserving
them.
It is in this light that we view freedom
of navigation. A waterway is not mereily
a security issue of concern for coastal
states. It is an artery of development
through which
the food,
medicine and energy of entire nations
flaw. When a single waterway is
disrupted, the cost is felt by a family
in a country that does not have a
coastline.
An economy that is difficult to disrupt
is difficult to coersse and
interdependence once firmly established
becomes a shield against coercion.
This approach is not a position shaped
by the current circumstances.
It is what his majesty King Huh bin isa
al- Khalifa king of the kingdom of
Bahrain has consistently advocated for
out of his majesty's conviction that the
security and prosperity of this region
are two faces of a single truth and that
a just peace and lasting stability are
the path towards a dignified life for
all the peoples of the region, whatever
their faiths or cultures.
Thus, we reaffirm that what the United
Nations needs today is not more
resolutions,
but greater capacity to implement them.
A resolution adopted but not implemented
has no value. and a right that is
recognized but not protected has no
value or meaning. I conclude by stating
that the kingdom of Bahrain continues to
be guided by his majesty's vision for
peace
as his majesty sees it is not declared
but built.
It can rest only on
the respect for human beings dignities
and beliefs. It should be built on
dialogue, not concession
or strength. The kingdom will remain
faithful to its international
commitments and covenants, committed to
international law, to freedom of
navigation, and to a just,
comprehensive, and lasting peace. True
to his majesty's approach, and
to the conviction that the security of
our region and the prosperity of its
peoples are a shared responsibility that
can only be safeguarded through our
collective effort. We pray to Almighty
God to grant this session every success
and to bestow upon our peoples and all
humanity security, peace, development
and prosperity. Thank you and peace be
upon you.
